newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lead market tightens despite falling LME tags.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lead market tightens despite falling LME tags.

text.p: U.S. lead supplies are tightening as the market moves into its seasonally strong period of consumption despite weakness in London Metal Exchange prices.

Although the benchmark LME three-month price fell earlier this week to a low of $566 a tonne from a high of $674.50 a month ago, the U.S. spot premium has moved up over the same timeframe to 2.50-3.50 cents from 1.50-2.00 cents on strong demand.

"The lead market continues to tighten in the U.S.," said David Cook, marketing consultant with Lake Engineering. "This is the time that battery demand kicks in. The producers are very tight. And there's not a lot of scrap around."
All of the primary producers in North America are believed to be turning away spot customers and only meeting contractual obligations.
"We're sold-out through October," said Tom Schnull, manager of lead products with Noranda Inc. "Between now and December, we expect the market to tighten further."
Battery production, which accounts for 70 percent of lead demand, begins in September and typically continues through January.

Noranda is also scheduled to take its 115,000-tonne-per-year Belledune smelter down in the second and third weeks of September for planned maintanence. "That will exacerbate the situation," said Thomas Parker, lead commodities purchasing manager for Exide Corp, the world's largest battery maker.
RSR Corp is bringing its Indianapolis secondary smelter back from a three-week shutdown, one week longer than originally planned. The smelter has a annual capacity of 114,000 tonnes.
The company's Los Angeles smelter is planning a two-week shutdown "within the next couple of months," said Bob Finn, RSR's president.

Lead production at Cominco Ltd's Trail smelter in the first half of the year is off 22.4 percent to 40,400 tonnes from last year's corresponding period, as the old lead facility was phased out to make way for the Kivcet smelter, which is still experiencing start-up glitches with its furnace.
A Cominco spokesman expected full production at is expected "within two or three months."
The other remaining primary producers, Asarco Inc and Doe Run, are also believed to be sold-out.
Dealers are finding little solace in the scrap market. "That's real issue for us," said RSR's Finn. "The milder winter means that not as many batteries failed, which leads to a tighter scrap market."
Battery scrap prices jumped to 7.5-8.5 cents over LME cash in the last two months from 6.5-7.5 cents.
So if the market is so strong fundamentally, why has the price fallen 16 percent in one month?
"The funds came in and hit lead pretty hard," Cook said. "It was mostly for technical reasons. But the fact is that the trade has been steady buyers."

"The lead premium is a better gauge of North American demand than the LME price," said Noranda's Schnull. "The LME price reflects a world price. And lead demand in Europe and the Far East is still pretty soft."

Cook agreed, saying, "The Canadian producers and the Mexicans typically export to the Far East and Europe. But the U.S. is the best market in the world right now. So producers that would normally be shipping offshore are sending material to the U.S."
